object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A recorded event describing a service outage or degradation that requires investigation and remediation. An incident exists from the moment someone declares it, and remains in the system indefinitely for historical tracking.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number. Unique and never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence... Unique.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal of a potential incident detected by monitoring systems or manually raised by an engineer. An alert is the monitoring platform's record of an anomaly and serves as one possible origin for an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, assigned by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support request or issue report. Tickets can originate as customer reports and may result in incident declarations.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a ticket in the support system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A named system or capability that can experience outages or degradation. Services are the units that incidents affect and that teams own.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a service within the service catalogue.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: An organizational unit responsible for owning and maintaining one or more services.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: TeamName
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a team.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: A person who can serve as an incident commander during an incident response.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: PersonId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a person.

source_references.excerpt: One person, named

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A measure of the technical impact and blast radius of an incident, ranging from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, one region). Independent of priority.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A measure of customer urgency and commercial impact, ranging from P1 (highest customer impact) to P4 (lowest). Independent of severity and determined by support based on who is affected and SLA considerations.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4... Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

ambiguities.description: Commander Optionality: The rule states that declared incidents must have exactly one commander, but triage incidents have none. However, the transcript does not clarify when an incident transitions from triage to declared state, nor does it specify whether an incident without a commander (in triage) can later acquire a commander. Is the commander assignment mandatory at declaration time, or can an incident be declared without one and have a commander assigned later?

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared. If it turns out to be nothing, it gets closed from triage having never had one... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority Change History: The transcript states that severity can change during an incident and that 'changes exist in the timeline' as events, but the model captures only the current severity and priority. Should the model include a fact type to capture historical severity and priority values with timestamps, or is it acceptable to store only the current state with the understanding that complete change history is available via a separate timeline system?

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate Chain Prevention: The transcript indicates that incident duplicates should form a direct hierarchy (B duplicates A, C duplicates A) with no chains (B duplicates A, C duplicates B). However, the system does not enforce this rule. Should the model capture this as an acyclic constraint on the 'is duplicate of' relationship, or acknowledge it as a business rule that is currently not enforced?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B?... It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain... So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything... It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Customer-Caused Incident Classification: The conversation discusses the possibility of reclassifying incidents that are later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration. This decision is deferred to a product/business leader (Ravi) and is not yet modeled. Should the model reserve a concept for incident cause classification, or remain purely at the current-state model without this dimension?

source_references.excerpt: Some of those tickets become incidents... turn out to be user error... once we know, that incident is in the numbers... Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided... because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Service Ownership Cardinality (Reverse): The transcript states that 'a service is owned by exactly one team,' but does not explicitly state whether a team can own zero services, one service, or multiple services. Is the reverse cardinality constrained?

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Alert Lifecycle and Incident Linkage: The transcript distinguishes between automated alerts from monitoring and manual alerts raised by engineers, but does not clarify whether every alert must eventually be linked to an incident, or whether an alert can exist without ever triggering an incident. Is alert creation dependent on incident creation, or can alerts exist independently?

source_references.excerpt: An engineer's looking at a dashboard for another reason and spots something... If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record... There's no path to an incident that doesn't have either an alert or a customer report behind it.

ambiguities.description: Ticket-to-Incident Conversion: The transcript mentions that 'some of those tickets become incidents' but does not clarify whether a ticket can generate multiple incidents, or whether an incident must trace back to exactly one ticket. Is the cardinality of the relationship between Tickets and Incidents one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many?

source_references.excerpt: Alert fires, someone declares. Two minutes later someone else who hasn't seen the channel declares another one for the same thing. Support gets tickets and declares a third. Now you've got three incidents for one event.

ambiguities.description: Person Identification: The transcript refers to the incident commander as 'one person, named,' but does not provide explicit details about how a Person is uniquely identified in the system. Is the identifier an employee ID, email address, name, or some other system-generated ID? The current model assumes a generic 'person_id' but this is not confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.
